database_summary: Classic Sakila-like DVD rental schema in SQLite. Contains entities for people/locations (actor, staff, customer, address, city, country), film catalog (film, language, category, film_category, film_actor, film_text), inventory & transactions (inventory, rental, payment, store) and small lookup tables. Mix of stable descriptive tables (country, language, category), stateful current entities (customer, staff, store, address, city), and event/history tables (rental, payment, inventory as inventory snapshots). Row counts indicate small reference tables and larger event tables (payments ~16k, rentals ~16k, inventory ~4.5k).

accepted.name: customer_full_address
accepted.body_sql:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.store_id,
       c.first_name,
       c.last_name,
       c.email,
       c.address_id,
       a.address,
       a.address2,
       a.district,
       a.city_id,
       ci.city,
       ci.country_id,
       co.country,
       a.postal_code,
       a.phone,
       c.active,
       c.create_date,
       c.last_update
FROM customer c
LEFT JOIN address a ON a.address_id = c.address_id
LEFT JOIN city ci ON ci.city_id = a.city_id
LEFT JOIN country co ON co.country_id = ci.country_id
accepted.description: One-row-per-customer enriched with their address, city and country names. Use this to answer customer location, contact, or segmentation questions and to join customers to geographic hierarchies. | Use for: List customers by city/country or district; Count customers per country/city; Find contact details for a customer or customers in a location; Join customers to payments/rentals by geography

accepted.name: film_with_category_and_language
accepted.body_sql:
SELECT f.film_id,
       f.title,
       f.description,
       f.release_year,
       f.language_id,
       l.name AS name,
       f.original_language_id,
       f.rental_duration,
       f.rental_rate,
       f.length,
       f.replacement_cost,
       f.rating,
       f.special_features,
       fc.category_id,
       cat.name AS category_name,
       f.last_update
FROM film f
LEFT JOIN language l ON l.language_id = f.language_id
LEFT JOIN film_category fc ON fc.film_id = f.film_id
LEFT JOIN category cat ON cat.category_id = fc.category_id
accepted.description: One-row-per-film with its primary language name and one category per row (films with multiple categories will have multiple rows). Useful for catalogue reporting, category counts, and joins to inventory/rental. | Use for: Count films by category or language; Find films in a category or language; Join film attributes to inventory/rental for revenue analysis

accepted.name: inventory_with_film_store
accepted.body_sql:
SELECT i.inventory_id,
       i.film_id,
       f.title AS title,
       i.store_id,
       s.address_id AS address_id,
       i.last_update
FROM inventory i
LEFT JOIN film f ON f.film_id = i.film_id
LEFT JOIN store s ON s.store_id = i.store_id
accepted.description: One-row-per-inventory item with film title and store address identifiers. Useful when analyzing rentals or stock by film and store. | Use for: Inventory counts by film/store; Join rentals/payments to film and store; Find which store holds copies of a film

accepted.name: payments_by_customer
accepted.body_sql:
SELECT p.customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS payment_count,
       SUM(p.amount) AS total_amount,
       MIN(p.payment_date) AS first_payment_date,
       MAX(p.payment_date) AS last_payment_date
FROM payment p
GROUP BY p.customer_id
accepted.description: Aggregated payment metrics per customer: total amount, payment_count, first and last payment date. Use this for customer lifetime value, recency/frequency/monetary (RFM) analysis and to join to customer demographics. | Use for: Compute total payments per customer; RFM segmentation; Identify top paying customers (join to RANK CTE)

accepted.name: rentals_enriched
accepted.body_sql:
SELECT r.rental_id,
       r.rental_date,
       r.inventory_id,
       i.film_id,
       f.title AS title,
       r.customer_id,
       r.return_date,
       r.staff_id,
       r.last_update,
       i.store_id
FROM rental r
LEFT JOIN inventory i ON i.inventory_id = r.inventory_id
LEFT JOIN film f ON f.film_id = i.film_id
accepted.description: One-row-per-rental event enriched with customer, inventory, film, staff and store identifiers for easy event-level analysis (revenue, duration, staff performance). Keep return_date to compute rental durations downstream. | Use for: Compute rental durations and delays; Analyze rentals by film, store, staff, or customer; Join rentals to payments or inventory availability

accepted.name: customer_payment_rfm
accepted.body_sql:
SELECT p.customer_id,
       COUNT(p.payment_id) AS payment_count,
       SUM(p.amount) AS monetary_value,
       MIN(p.payment_date) AS first_payment_date,
       MAX(p.payment_date) AS last_payment_date
FROM payment p
GROUP BY p.customer_id
accepted.description: RFM-style aggregated measures per customer combining payment totals and recency/frequency measures. Useful for customer segmentation and deriving monetary/recency/frequency flags. | Use for: Customer lifetime value; Segment customers by recency/frequency/monetary; Identify customers with declining payments

accepted.name: film_actor_counts
accepted.body_sql:
SELECT fa.film_id,
       COUNT(fa.actor_id) AS actor_count
FROM film_actor fa
GROUP BY fa.film_id
accepted.description: Count of actors per film and count of films per actor (two separate aggregations exposed as rows keyed by film_id or actor_id). Useful for casting-related queries and measuring actor/film breadth. | Use for: Find films with many or few actors; Join actor counts to film catalog or inventory

accepted.name: actor_film_counts
accepted.body_sql:
SELECT fa.actor_id,
       COUNT(fa.film_id) AS film_count
FROM film_actor fa
GROUP BY fa.actor_id
accepted.description: Number of films each actor appears in. Useful for actor-centric leaderboards and casting analytics. | Use for: Top actors by film appearances; Filter actors by number of films

accepted.name: payments_running_total_by_customer
accepted.body_sql:
SELECT p.payment_id,
       p.customer_id,
       p.payment_date,
       p.amount,
       SUM(p.amount) OVER (PARTITION BY p.customer_id ORDER BY p.payment_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total_amount,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.customer_id ORDER BY p.payment_date DESC) AS payment_rank
FROM payment p
accepted.description: Payments ordered by payment_date per customer with a running total and a payment_rank. Useful for computing recency and cumulative spend sequences or to implement Top-K most recent payments per customer by filtering payment_rank. | Use for: Cumulative spend per customer over time; Select most recent N payments per customer using payment_rank; Identify when customers reached spending milestones

accepted.name: latest_payment_per_customer
accepted.body_sql:
SELECT p.payment_id,
       p.customer_id,
       p.payment_date,
       p.amount,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.customer_id ORDER BY p.payment_date DESC) AS payment_rank
FROM payment p
accepted.description: Latest payment row per customer (one row per customer with their most recent payment). Useful to compute recency or to join latest payment details to customer records. This CTE exposes payment_rank so consumers can change which rank to select. | Use for: Get latest payment per customer (WHERE payment_rank = 1); Compute recency by joining payment_date to today

accepted.name: store_staff_roster
accepted.body_sql:
SELECT s.staff_id,
       s.first_name,
       s.last_name,
       s.address_id,
       a.address,
       a.city_id,
       s.email,
       s.store_id,
       s.active,
       s.username,
       s.last_update
FROM staff s
LEFT JOIN address a ON a.address_id = s.address_id
accepted.description: One-row-per-staff member including their store and address identifiers and contact info. Useful for staff performance, manager lookups, and store-level joins. | Use for: List staff by store or city; Join staff to rentals/payments for performance metrics
